# Fine-Tuning and Evaluation {#instruction-fine-tuning-and-evaluation}

There are three ways to make a pre-trained model better at your task. Each one
changes something different:

| Lever | What changes | Covered in |
|:------|:-------------|:-----------|
| Prompting and in-context learning | Only the input; the weights stay fixed | Section \@ref(prompt-engineering) and the Prompt Engineering part |
| Fine-tuning | The weights, using labelled examples | This chapter |
| Alignment with human feedback | The weights, using preference signals | Next chapter |

This chapter covers supervised fine-tuning: full instruction fine-tuning first,
then parameter-efficient methods. It ends with how to measure whether the
adapted model actually improved.

## Why fine-tune instead of prompting

In-context learning puts worked examples in the prompt (Section
\@ref(prompt-engineering)). It needs no training, so it should be tried first.
It has four limits:

- **Small models may not pick up the task**, even from several examples.
- **Examples use up the context window**, leaving less room for the actual
  input, retrieved documents, or tool results.
- **Examples are paid for on every call**, in tokens and in latency.
- **Prompts are not great at fixing a style or format** across thousands of
  calls. Training on examples usually makes the output more consistent.

Fine-tuning moves the task knowledge from the prompt into the weights. A
practical rule of thumb: fine-tuning is good at teaching **behaviour** (a task,
format, style, or domain vocabulary). It is a poor way to add **facts that
change**. Fresh or private facts are better supplied at inference time through
retrieval, which a later chapter covers.

**Example: one marketing assistant, three needs.**

| Need | Best lever | Why |
|:-----|:-----------|:----|
| Always write in the brand's voice and house format | Fine-tuning | Stable behaviour, needed on every call |
| Quote this week's promotions and prices | Retrieval | Facts that change weekly |
| Handle an unusual one-off request | Prompting | No training data, and it may never recur |

> **In short.**
>
> - Try prompting first; fine-tune when examples don't work, eat the
>   context window, cost too much per call, or give inconsistent output.
> - Fine-tuning teaches behaviour; retrieval supplies changing facts.

## Instruction fine-tuning

**Instruction fine-tuning** (also called supervised fine-tuning, SFT) continues
training a pre-trained model on pairs. Each pair is a prompt containing an
instruction plus the desired completion:

```text
Prompt:     Classify this review: "I loved this book, could not put it down."
Completion: Sentiment: positive
```

It differs from pre-training in two ways. Pre-training is self-supervised on
unlabelled text. Instruction fine-tuning is supervised on labelled pairs, and
the dataset is many orders of magnitude smaller. When every weight is updated,
the procedure is called **full fine-tuning**. Its output is a new copy of the
model, often called an *instruct model*.

### Building the dataset

Most existing NLP datasets (reviews, Q&A pairs, dialogues) are not written as
instructions. **Prompt template libraries** such as PromptSource
[@bach2022promptsource] solve this. A template wraps each record in an
instruction. For example, an Amazon review can become a rating-prediction
prompt, a review-generation prompt, or a summarization prompt.

Using **several phrasings of the same instruction** ("Summarize the
dialogue", "What was this conversation about?", ...) helps the model generalize
beyond one wording. The original FLAN work wrote ten templates per dataset for
this reason [@wei2022flan].

Split the data into training, validation, and test sets, as in any supervised
problem. The test set must stay untouched until the final evaluation.

### Training objective

The model is trained with the same next-token cross-entropy loss used in
pre-training, applied to the completion. For a prompt $x$ and target completion
$y = (y_1, \dots, y_T)$:

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta\left(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}\right)
$$

The loss is commonly computed only on the completion tokens. The prompt tokens
are masked out, so the model is not trained to reproduce the instruction.
For the review example above:

```text
Tokens:   Classify this review: "I loved this book ..."  Sentiment: positive
In loss:  no       no   no      no  no   no   no   ...   yes        yes
```

The model still reads the whole sequence, but only the completion tokens
produce gradients.
Gradients from batches of examples update the weights over one or more epochs.
The validation loss or metric is tracked to choose when to stop.

Full fine-tuning has the same memory profile as training. Weights, gradients,
and optimizer states must all fit in memory (Section
\@ref(memory-challenges-in-training-llms)). That cost motivates the
parameter-efficient methods in Section \@ref(peft).

> **In short.**
>
> - Instruction fine-tuning is supervised next-token training on
>   prompt–completion pairs, with the loss usually on the completion only.
> - Templates turn existing datasets into instructions; several phrasings
>   per task help generalization.
> - Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs training-level memory.

## Single-task fine-tuning and catastrophic forgetting

If an application needs only one task, such as summarizing support chats, you
can fine-tune on that task alone. Single-task fine-tuning often works with
**hundreds to a few thousand** high-quality examples. That is tiny compared
with pre-training corpora. LIMA, for example, reported strong instruction
following after tuning on 1,000 curated examples [@zhou2023lima]. Treat any
number as a starting point to validate, not a requirement. Label quality and
representativeness matter more than volume.

The risk is **catastrophic forgetting**: updating the weights for one task can
degrade abilities learned earlier [@mccloskey1989catastrophic]. For example, a
model tuned only for sentiment classification may stop doing named-entity
recognition correctly, or may answer every prompt with a sentiment label.

Ways to handle it, roughly in order of cost:

1. **Check whether it matters.** If the deployed model only ever performs the
   tuned task, losing other skills may be acceptable.
2. **Mix in general data.** Add a sample of general instruction data (or the
   earlier tasks) to the fine-tuning set. This is sometimes called *replay*.
3. **Regularize the update.** Penalize movement of weights that mattered for
   earlier tasks, for example with elastic weight consolidation
   [@kirkpatrick2017ewc].
4. **Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning.** Freeze the original weights and
   train a small add-on (Section \@ref(peft)).
5. **Fine-tune on many tasks at once** (next section).

Whatever you choose, evaluate **both** the target task and a fixed set of
capabilities you need to keep. Without the second set, forgetting goes
unnoticed.

> **In short.**
>
> - One task often needs only hundreds to a few thousand good examples.
> - The risk is catastrophic forgetting of other skills.
> - Mitigate with replay, regularization, PEFT, or multi-task training, and
>   always measure retained capabilities.

## Multi-task instruction fine-tuning and FLAN

**Multi-task instruction fine-tuning** trains on a mixture of tasks
(summarization, classification, translation, question answering, code, ...) at
the same time. Because no single task dominates, the model improves across many
tasks instead of trading them off. The cost is data: you need diverse,
high-quality examples for every task in the mixture.

The FLAN models are the reference example (FLAN stands for *Fine-tuned LAnguage
Net*):

- @wei2022flan fine-tuned a 137B-parameter model on more than 60 datasets
  phrased as instructions. Its *zero-shot* performance improved on task types
  that were **held out** of training. This was the key evidence that instruction
  tuning teaches the general skill of following instructions, not just the
  training tasks.
- @chung2022scaling scaled the approach to **1,836 tasks** (drawn from 473
  datasets in 146 task categories) and released Flan-T5 and Flan-PaLM. Two
  findings matter: performance kept improving as both the number of tasks and
  the model size grew, and including chain-of-thought examples in the mixture
  preserved the models' step-by-step reasoning ability. Instruction tuning
  was also cheap: for Flan-PaLM 540B it used about 0.2% of the pre-training
  compute.

The Flan 2022 paper uses three terms precisely [@chung2022scaling]:

- a **dataset** is an original data source, such as SQuAD;
- a **task category** is a kind of task setup, such as extractive question
  answering or question generation (one dataset can serve several);
- a **task** is one (dataset, task category) pair, such as question
  generation on SQuAD, with any number of instruction templates.

The fine-tuning mixture combined four collections, and evaluation used
benchmarks kept out of training:

| Collection | Datasets | Task categories | Tasks | What it adds |
|:-----------|---------:|----------------:|------:|:-------------|
| Muffin | 69 | 27 | 80 | The original FLAN tasks plus dialogue and program synthesis |
| T0-SF | 55 | 14 | 193 | Tasks from T0 that do not overlap with Muffin ("sans Flan") |
| Natural Instructions v2 | 372 | 108 | 1,554 | A large crowd-sourced task collection (MMLU-related tasks removed) |
| CoT | 9 | 1 | 9 | Reasoning tasks with human-written chains of thought |
| **Total** | **473** | **146** | **1,836** | Some datasets appear in more than one collection |

| Held-out benchmark | What it tests | Size |
|:-------------------|:--------------|:-----|
| MMLU | Exam-style knowledge across subjects | 57 tasks |
| BBH (BIG-Bench Hard) | Hard reasoning tasks where models trailed average human raters | 23 tasks (27 subtasks) |
| TyDiQA | Information-seeking question answering | 8 languages |
| MGSM | Grade-school math word problems | 10 languages |

The point of the split is the claim being tested. A gain on tasks the model
never saw during fine-tuning is evidence that it learned to follow
instructions in general, not just the training tasks. The authors removed 44
MMLU-related tasks from the training mixture for exactly this reason.

One dataset in the FLAN mixture is **SAMSum**: about 16,000 messenger-style
dialogues with summaries, written by linguists [@gliwa2019samsum]. It explains
both the strength and the limit of a general instruct model. Flan-T5 can
summarize casual chats between friends. However, a customer-support dialogue
has a different structure (a customer request, staff actions, a resolution).
A general model may miss key actions or invent details there.

The fix is a further round of fine-tuning on data close to the deployment
setting. **DialogSum** is a public example: about 13,000 dialogues from
real-life scenarios such as hotel check-ins and service desks, each with a
summary [@chen2021dialogsum]. In production, permissioned internal data (your
own support transcripts and the summaries your team wants) is usually the
better choice. Even then, evaluate hallucination, privacy, and distribution
shift separately.

> **In short.**
>
> - Training on many tasks at once improves many tasks instead of trading
>   them off.
> - FLAN's evidence: gains on benchmarks held out of training, so the model
>   learned to follow instructions in general.
> - A general instruct model may still need a further round of tuning on
>   data close to your deployment.

## Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) {#peft}

Full fine-tuning has three practical costs:

1. **Training memory.** Gradients and optimizer states are needed for every
   parameter. With Adam, that is several times the memory of the weights
   themselves.
2. **Storage.** Each task produces a complete copy of the model.
3. **Forgetting.** Every weight can move, which risks catastrophic forgetting.

**Parameter-efficient fine-tuning** methods freeze most or all of the
pre-trained weights and train a small number of parameters. That reduces the
gradient and optimizer memory. The task-specific artefact can be a few
megabytes instead of a full model. The frozen base also makes forgetting less
likely.

Note what PEFT does *not* remove: the frozen weights must still sit in memory
for the forward and backward passes. QLoRA (below) attacks that remaining
cost.

### Three families of methods

@lialin2023scaling group PEFT methods into three families:

| Family | Idea | Examples |
|:-------|:-----|:---------|
| **Selective** | Train only a chosen subset of the existing parameters | BitFit trains only the bias terms [@benzaken2022bitfit]; training only the top layers |
| **Reparameterization** | Learn the weight *update* in a compact, low-rank form | LoRA [@hu2022lora] |
| **Additive** | Keep the original weights frozen and add new trainable parameters | Adapter layers inserted inside each block [@houlsby2019adapters]; soft prompts [@lester2021prompt; @li2021prefix] |

Selective methods are simple. They are less common for large generative models
because their quality and memory savings vary a lot. The two methods most used
in practice are LoRA and soft prompts. Both are explained below.

### LoRA: low-rank adaptation

**Idea.** Full fine-tuning learns an update $\Delta W$ for each weight matrix
$W_0$. @hu2022lora hypothesized that this update has low *intrinsic rank*. If
so, it can be written as the product of two thin matrices. LoRA freezes $W_0$
and trains only those two matrices:

$$
h = W_0 x + \Delta W x = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x,
\qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\;
A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\;
r \ll \min(d, k)
$$

- $r$ is the **rank**, the main hyperparameter. $\alpha$ is a scaling
  constant.
- $A$ starts random and $B$ starts at zero. At step 0, $\Delta W = 0$, so
  training begins exactly at the pre-trained model.
- Only $A$ and $B$ get gradients and optimizer states.

**Parameter count.** A $d \times k$ matrix has $dk$ parameters. Its LoRA update
has $r(d + k)$.

| Matrix | Full update $dk$ | LoRA, $r = 8$: $r(d+k)$ | Share trained |
|:-------|-----------------:|------------------------:|--------------:|
| One attention head projection in the original Transformer, $512 \times 64$ [@vaswani2017attention] | 32,768 | 4,608 | 14% |
| A $4096 \times 4096$ projection, typical of a 7B-parameter model | 16,777,216 | 65,536 | 0.39% |

The savings grow with the matrix size. On GPT-3 175B, @hu2022lora reported
about **10,000× fewer trainable parameters** and about **3× lower GPU memory**
than full fine-tuning. Quality was on par with or better than full fine-tuning
on the tasks they evaluated.

**Inference.** After training, the update can be merged into the base weights,
$W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA$. The merged model has exactly the original
shape, so it adds **no inference latency**. Alternatively, keep the adapters
separate and load a different $(A, B)$ pair per task on one shared base model.
That is how one deployment can serve many tasks.

**Which matrices to adapt.** The LoRA paper adapted the attention projections
(mainly the query and value matrices). It found that adapting more matrix types
at a small rank beat adapting one type at a larger rank [@hu2022lora]. Despite
a common claim, attention does *not* hold most of a transformer's parameters.
With the usual feed-forward width of $4d$, the feed-forward layers hold about
two-thirds of each block's weights. The QLoRA authors found that applying LoRA
to **all linear layers** was needed to match full fine-tuning
[@dettmers2023qlora].

**Choosing the rank.** In @hu2022lora, very small ranks (even single digits)
were competitive on the tasks studied. Raising the rank did not reliably help.
Values from 4 to 64 are common in practice. Treat $r$ (and $\alpha$) as
hyperparameters to tune on the validation set. A larger rank means more
capacity and more memory, not automatically better results.

### QLoRA: LoRA on a quantized base

LoRA shrinks the trainable part, but the frozen base model still has to fit in
memory. **QLoRA** stores the frozen base in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA
adapters in 16-bit on top of it [@dettmers2023qlora]. Three techniques make
this work:

- **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)**, a 4-bit data type designed for weights that are
  roughly normally distributed.
- **Double quantization**, which also quantizes the quantization constants to
  save more memory.
- **Paged optimizers**, which move optimizer state to CPU memory during memory
  spikes.

The paper fine-tuned a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU while
preserving the task performance of 16-bit fine-tuning. Section
\@ref(quantization-techniques) explains the data types involved.

### Prompt tuning with soft prompts

**Prompt tuning** is not prompt engineering. Prompt engineering edits the words
of a prompt by hand. Prompt tuning *learns* a short sequence of continuous
vectors, a **soft prompt**, that is prepended to the input embeddings
[@lester2021prompt]:

- Ordinary ("hard") tokens map to fixed rows of the embedding table. A soft
  prompt is $p$ *virtual tokens*: free vectors $P \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times d}$
  in the same embedding space, not tied to any word.
- The model is completely frozen. Backpropagation updates only $P$, using the
  same supervised loss as fine-tuning.
- The trainable count is tiny. Twenty virtual tokens with $d = 4096$ is 81,920
  parameters. One soft prompt per task can be stored and swapped at inference,
  and a single batch can even mix tasks.

**Evidence.** On SuperGLUE, prompt tuning trailed full fine-tuning for small
T5 models. The gap closed as model size grew, and at about 11B parameters it
matched full fine-tuning. It also outperformed GPT-3's few-shot prompting by a
large margin. In the
same experiments, about 20 virtual tokens captured most of the gain; longer
prompts added little [@lester2021prompt].

**Interpretability.** The learned vectors do not correspond to vocabulary
tokens. Their nearest vocabulary neighbours tend to form semantically related
clusters, often connected to the task. Even so, a soft prompt cannot be read
like a sentence.

**Related method.** *Prefix tuning* learns trainable vectors at every layer, not
only at the input, giving it more capacity per virtual token [@li2021prefix].

### Choosing an adaptation method

| Method | Trainable parameters | Training memory | Inference overhead | Typical use |
|:-------|:---------------------|:----------------|:-------------------|:------------|
| Prompting / in-context learning | None | None | Longer prompts | First attempt; fast iteration |
| Full fine-tuning | All | Highest | None | Large shift in behaviour, enough data and compute |
| LoRA | Well under 1% for large models (depends on rank and layers) | Low (base still in memory) | None if merged | Default PEFT choice; many tasks on one base |
| QLoRA | Same as LoRA | Lowest (4-bit base) | None if merged; quantized base otherwise | Large models on limited GPUs |
| Prompt tuning | Tiny ($p \times d$) | Low | A few extra input positions | Very large frozen models; many tasks |

> **Current practice (October 2026).** LoRA and QLoRA remain the standard
> PEFT methods in common open-source tooling, such as the Hugging Face `peft`
> library. Many hosted model APIs offer fine-tuning without exposing the
> method. Supervised fine-tuning is now usually one stage in a pipeline that
> also includes preference-based alignment (next chapter).

> **In short.**
>
> - PEFT freezes most weights and trains a small add-on: less memory, tiny
>   task files, less forgetting.
> - LoRA learns a low-rank update $BA$, mergeable with no inference cost;
>   apply it to all linear layers.
> - QLoRA adds a 4-bit frozen base; prompt tuning learns input vectors and
>   catches up with full fine-tuning at large scale.

## Evaluating fine-tuned models {#evaluating-model-performance-in-language-tasks}

Classifier accuracy is easy to compute because there is one right label.
Generated text is harder to score. Two sentences can mean the same thing with
almost no shared words ("Mike really loves drinking tea" vs. "Mike adores
sipping tea"). Two others can differ by one word and mean the opposite ("Mike
does drink coffee" vs. "Mike does not drink coffee"). Automatic metrics
approximate quality through overlap with a human **reference**. That makes them
cheap and repeatable, but blind to meaning.

Terminology: a **unigram** is one word, a **bigram** is two consecutive words,
and an **n-gram** is $n$ consecutive words.

### ROUGE

**ROUGE** [@lin2004rouge] scores summaries by their overlap with reference
summaries. For n-gram matches between a candidate and a reference:

$$
\text{Recall} = \frac{\text{matched n-grams}}{\text{n-grams in reference}},
\qquad
\text{Precision} = \frac{\text{matched n-grams}}{\text{n-grams in candidate}},
\qquad
F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R}
$$

- **ROUGE-1** uses unigrams, **ROUGE-2** uses bigrams (which are slightly
  sensitive to word order).
- **ROUGE-L** uses the length of the **longest common subsequence** (LCS) as
  the match count. A subsequence keeps word order but does *not* have to be
  contiguous. Mixing this up with the longest contiguous match is a common
  error.

**Worked example.** Reference: *"It is cold outside"* (4 words). Candidate:
*"It is very cold outside"* (5 words).

| Metric | Matches | Recall | Precision | F1 |
|:-------|:--------|-------:|----------:|---:|
| ROUGE-1 | it, is, cold, outside = 4 | 4/4 = 1.00 | 4/5 = 0.80 | 0.89 |
| ROUGE-2 | "it is", "cold outside" = 2 | 2/3 = 0.67 | 2/4 = 0.50 | 0.57 |
| ROUGE-L | LCS "it is cold outside" = 4 | 4/4 = 1.00 | 4/5 = 0.80 | 0.89 |

**Failure modes:**

- **Meaning reversal.** *"It is not cold outside"* gets exactly the same ROUGE-1
  scores as the candidate above. Overlap does not check meaning.
- **Repetition.** *"cold cold cold cold"* has a ROUGE-1 precision of 4/4 =
  1.00 if every repeat counts. **Clipping** caps each n-gram's matches at its
  count in the reference. The idea comes from BLEU's modified precision
  [@papineni2002bleu]. With clipping, precision becomes 1/4 = 0.25.
- **Reordering.** *"outside cold it is"* still scores 1.00 on clipped ROUGE-1.
  Order-sensitive variants catch it: ROUGE-2 F1 = 1/3 = 0.33 (only "it is"
  matches) and ROUGE-L F1 = 0.50 (LCS = 2).

ROUGE scores are comparable only within the same task, dataset, reference set,
and implementation settings (tokenization, stemming). Use them to track
progress on summarization while you iterate, never as the final verdict.

### BLEU

**BLEU** [@papineni2002bleu] was designed for machine translation. It is
precision-oriented and combines several n-gram sizes:

$$
\text{BLEU} = \text{BP} \cdot \exp\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N} w_n \log p_n\right),
\qquad
\text{BP} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } c > r \\
e^{\,1 - r/c} & \text{if } c \le r
\end{cases}
$$

- $p_n$ is the **clipped** n-gram precision. Usually $N = 4$ with equal
  weights $w_n = 1/4$, so the exponential term is the *geometric mean* of the
  four precisions (not a simple average).
- The **brevity penalty** BP penalizes candidates shorter than the reference
  ($c$ = candidate length, $r$ = reference length). Without it, a very short
  output with only safe words would score high precision.
- BLEU was defined at the corpus level. Sentence-level BLEU is noisy and needs
  smoothing, because a single missing 4-gram makes the geometric mean zero.

For example, a 4-word translation against a 5-word reference gets
$\text{BP} = e^{1 - 5/4} \approx 0.78$. Even with perfect n-gram precision,
its BLEU cannot exceed 0.78.

### Beyond overlap metrics

ROUGE and BLEU are cheap diagnostics. They cannot judge factual correctness,
faithfulness to the source, safety, or usefulness. A defensible evaluation
combines:

- a **representative held-out set** drawn from the deployment setting;
- **task-appropriate automatic metrics** (overlap, exact match, schema
  validity, executable tests);
- **structured human review** with a written rubric where judgment is needed;
- **error analysis** by category and subgroup;
- **retained-capability checks** to detect catastrophic forgetting; and
- latency and cost.

**LLM-as-a-judge** (using a strong model to grade outputs against a rubric)
scales human-like judgments cheaply. @zheng2023judge found that strong judges
agree with human preferences about as often as humans agree with each other.
They also documented systematic biases: position bias, a preference for longer
answers, and a tendency to favour the judge's own outputs. Calibrate a judge
against human labels before trusting it. Chapter
\@ref(evaluating-agentic-systems) shows how to do this, and how to build
rubric-based evals for multi-step systems.

> **In short.**
>
> - ROUGE (recall-leaning, summaries) and BLEU (precision plus brevity
>   penalty, translation) measure surface overlap with references.
> - They miss meaning, so use them for iteration, not as the final verdict.
> - Combine held-out data, task metrics, human or calibrated-judge review,
>   error analysis, and retained-capability checks.

## Benchmarks {#benchmarks}

Benchmarks are fixed, public task suites used to compare models across many
skills:

| Benchmark | Year | What it measures |
|:----------|:-----|:-----------------|
| GLUE [@wang2019glue] | 2018 | Nine sentence- and sentence-pair understanding tasks (sentiment, entailment, paraphrase, ...) |
| SuperGLUE [@wang2019superglue] | 2019 | Eight harder tasks (multi-sentence reasoning, reading comprehension, coreference), created as models saturated GLUE |
| MMLU [@hendrycks2021mmlu] | 2020 | Multiple-choice knowledge and problem-solving across 57 subjects (elementary mathematics, US history, law, computer science, ...) |
| BIG-bench [@srivastava2023bigbench] | 2022 | 204 community-contributed tasks (linguistics, common sense, mathematics, social bias, software, ...); a smaller "Lite" subset keeps evaluation cost manageable |
| HELM [@liang2023helm] | 2022 | A framework scoring models on seven metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) across 16 core scenarios, so trade-offs are visible rather than hidden in one number |

**How to read benchmark results:**

- **Saturation.** Top systems surpassed the SuperGLUE human-baseline estimate
  within about two years. A model matching humans on a benchmark is not human
  level at the general skill. This "arms race" is why benchmarks keep being
  replaced.
- **Contamination.** If test items appeared in the pre-training data, scores
  overstate ability. Prefer held-out or recently created items.
- **Fit.** A leaderboard rank says little about *your* task. A small
  evaluation set drawn from your own data is usually more informative.
- **Holistic view.** Accuracy alone hides calibration, robustness, and safety
  trade-offs, which is the point HELM was built to make.

> **Current practice (October 2026).** GLUE and SuperGLUE are of historical
> interest for frontier models, and MMLU is close to saturated. Harder
> successors such as MMLU-Pro [@wang2024mmlupro] and the expert-written GPQA
> [@rein2023gpqa] took their place, along with agentic and coding benchmarks
> and arena-style human-preference rankings. Leaderboards change quickly;
> check current sources before quoting a score.

> **In short.**
>
> - Benchmarks compare models on fixed public tasks: GLUE, SuperGLUE, MMLU,
>   BIG-bench, HELM.
> - Read them with care: saturation, contamination, and poor fit to your
>   task. Your own small eval set usually tells you more.

## Key takeaways

The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines:

- **When:** prompt first; fine-tune for behaviour, retrieve for facts.
- **How:** supervised next-token training on instruction pairs; many tasks
  at once (FLAN) generalize to held-out tasks.
- **Risk:** catastrophic forgetting; always test the skills you need to
  keep.
- **Cheaply:** PEFT, usually LoRA or QLoRA, trains under 1% of the
  parameters with no inference cost once merged.
- **Measured:** overlap metrics for iteration; held-out data, human or
  judge review, and error analysis for the verdict.

## Interview checkpoints

- **Fine-tuning vs. RAG?** Fine-tuning changes behaviour, format, and style.
  Retrieval supplies current or private facts at inference. They are often
  combined.
- **Why does LoRA add no inference latency?** The update $BA$ can be merged into
  $W_0$, so the deployed model has the original shape.
- **LoRA parameter count for a $d \times k$ matrix?** $r(d + k)$ instead of
  $dk$.
- **Why is $B$ initialized to zero?** So that $\Delta W = 0$ and training starts
  exactly at the pre-trained model.
- **What does QLoRA add?** A 4-bit NF4 frozen base, double quantization, and
  paged optimizers, so large models fit on one GPU.
- **Prompt tuning vs. prompt engineering?** Learned continuous vectors vs.
  hand-written discrete text. Prompt tuning needs training data and gradients.
- **What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you detect it?** Loss of
  earlier skills after fine-tuning. Detect it with a fixed retained-capability
  evaluation set.
- **ROUGE-L vs. ROUGE-2?** ROUGE-L uses the longest common *subsequence*
  (order-preserving, not contiguous). ROUGE-2 counts matching bigrams.
- **Why does BLEU need a brevity penalty?** Precision alone rewards very short
  outputs.
- **Why distrust a high benchmark score?** Saturation, contamination, and
  mismatch with the deployment task.
- **In FLAN, what is the difference between a dataset, a task category, and
  a task?** A dataset is a data source (SQuAD); a task category is a task
  setup (question generation); a task is one dataset–category pair.
- **How did Flan 2022 show that instruction tuning generalizes?** By
  evaluating on benchmarks held out of training (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA, MGSM),
  after removing overlapping tasks from the mixture.
